questions.question: A rounded fairing is added in the corner where the wing of an airliner meets the fuselage. Which kind of drag does it mainly reduce?
options: Interference drag, where the flows around the two parts meet
Induced drag, because the fairing changes the wing's lift
Wave drag, because the fairing weakens the shock waves
Skin friction drag, because the fairing covers part of the skin
questions.explanation: Where two parts meet, the flows around them collide and the pair has more drag than the two alone. That extra is interference drag, and a fairing in the corner reduces it. The fairing does not change the lift or the span, so the induced drag stays the same. Wave drag appears only near the speed of sound. A fairing adds a little wetted area, so it does not lower the skin friction.

questions.question: A round strut and a streamlined strut of the same thickness are tested in the same flow. Why does the round strut have much more drag?
options: The flow leaves its surface and forms a wide wake of low pressure behind it
It has more skin for the air to rub on, so its skin friction is larger
It makes lift as the air goes around it, so it has induced drag
The air speeds up around it, which raises the pressure on its back
questions.explanation: Behind a blunt body the boundary layer separates and leaves a wide wake whose pressure stays low, while the front feels a high pressure. The difference is the pressure drag. The streamlined strut keeps the flow attached and its wake thin. It has more wetted area than the round strut, not less. A symmetric strut in a straight flow makes no lift. Faster air has lower pressure, not higher.

questions.question: An aircraft has the drag polar CD = 0.016 + 0.050 CL2. What is its drag coefficient at CL = 0.4?
questions.explanation: CD = 0.016 + 0.050 × 0.42 = 0.016 + 0.008 = 0.024. 0.036 forgets to square CL; 0.008 is the induced part alone, without the zero-lift drag; 0.011 multiplies the sum of the two numbers by CL2.

questions.question: A drag polar is built from wind-tunnel measurements of lift and drag on a model. What does each point of the finished polar stand for?
options: One angle of attack of the model
One speed of the tunnel
One Reynolds number of the test
One weight of the aircraft
questions.explanation: The model is set at a series of angles of attack, and at each one the lift and the drag are measured. Each angle gives one pair of coefficients, one point of the polar; the angle itself no longer shows on the graph. The whole polar holds for one Reynolds number, so the tunnel speed is held fixed, and the weight of the aircraft plays no part in a tunnel test.

questions.question: Two airfoil sections of the same family and thickness differ only in camber: one is symmetric, the other cambered. Where does the cambered section have its lowest drag?
options: At a positive lift coefficient
At zero lift, as the symmetric one does
At a negative lift coefficient
At its maximum lift coefficient
questions.explanation: A symmetric section has its least drag at zero lift, and its polar is the same for positive and negative lift. Camber shifts the low-drag range to positive lift, where the section is meant to work. The cambered section on this page has its least drag between lift coefficients of about 0.26 and 0.88. Near the maximum lift coefficient the drag rises steeply.

questions.section: Drag against speed in steady level flight
questions.question: An airliner in steady level flight doubles its speed at the same altitude and weight. What happens to its parasite drag and its induced drag?
options: Parasite drag becomes 4 times larger; induced drag becomes 4 times smaller
Both become 4 times larger, because all drag grows with the speed squared
Parasite drag doubles; induced drag halves
Parasite drag becomes 4 times larger; induced drag stays the same
questions.explanation: In level flight D = qSCD,0 + KW2/(qS), with q = ½ρV2. Doubling V makes q 4 times larger: the parasite term grows 4 times and the induced term, which divides by q, falls to a quarter. The faster aircraft needs a lower lift coefficient, so its induced drag does not stay the same, and the dependence is on the square of the speed, not the speed itself.

questions.section: Minimum drag and the maximum lift-to-drag ratio
questions.question: An aircraft with CD,0 = 0.023 flies at its minimum-drag speed. What is its drag coefficient there?
questions.explanation: At minimum drag the lift coefficient is CL* = √(CD,0/K), so the induced part KCL*2 equals CD,0, and CD = 2 × 0.023 = 0.046. 0.023 is the zero-lift drag alone, the lowest point of the polar, where the aircraft would carry no weight. 0.0115 halves it, and 0.069 counts the induced part twice.

questions.section: Minimum drag and the maximum lift-to-drag ratio
questions.question: An aircraft has CD,0 = 0.016 and K = 0.040. What is its maximum lift-to-drag ratio?
questions.explanation: (L/D)max = 1/(2√(KCD,0)) = 1/(2√0.00064) = 1/(2 × 0.0253) = 19.8. 39.5 leaves out the 2; 781 leaves out the square root; 0.632 is CL* = √(0.016/0.040), the lift coefficient at which the maximum occurs, not the ratio itself.
